detail.longDescription: I would not park an agent on a free server until I can carry the whole run away. A friendly login and a warm machine can still hide the files, the tool transcript, and the prompt that produced a bad patch. If I cannot export those three things after one dry run, I treat that host as a sketchpad only. Would you trust a laptop you cannot image, just because the sticker on the lid says free? The question I keep returning to is not which invoice looks smaller at the end of this week. I ask who holds the workspace after the process exits, and who can wipe it without sending me a note. A self-hosted box and a paid isolated machine usually answer that with a disk I can still open tomorrow. A shared free server may answer it with a session that disappears when the operator reclaims the seat. Name the bundle before you name the host An exit bundle is the smallest folder that lets another machine audit my judgment, not the model's personality. I want the prompt file, the tool-call log, the workspace hashes, and a short note about commands I refused. If any of those pieces lives only inside a web console, I do not yet have a bundle I can defend. Have you ever tried to explain a failed agent run from memory alone, a week after the tab was closed? I borrowed the instinct from code review, not from a pricing page, because unclear runs waste the same hours as unclear patches. A clean diff can still be a murky story if nobody can see which tool fired and which tool was blocked. Comments in a pull request help a human, but they do not replace a log the agent host actually stored. So I ask a blunt question before I celebrate a demo: could a teammate rebuild this conclusion without my chat scrollback? Three seats, three custody stories I compare three seats before I fall in love with a signup flow, because the seat decides who can read the files later. The free shared seat is useful when the work is disposable and I can stand to lose the scratch directory. The self-hosted seat is useful when I already own the machine, the user account, and the backup job. The paid isolated seat is useful when I need a vendor boundary, a support path, and a disk I did not build. None of those seats is a moral winner, and I do not pretend a receipt proves better judgment. A free seat kept for a spike can quietly become the only home for the notes. That slide is the failure I want this drill to catch, rather than a slogan about hosts. If your notes already live in one browser profile, why would a new agent host be any kinder? Walk five steps on a fixture These five steps are a proposed workflow, not a report of a finished rollout on a named vendor. I am describing the checks I would run, and I am not claiming I already timed them in production. If a step feels obvious, I still want it written down, because obvious checks are the ones people skip. Have you skipped an export lately just because the diff looked small enough to trust on sight? 1. Freeze a tiny fixture I start with a fixture repo that contains one failing test, one allowed edit path, and one forbidden path. I do not point the agent at a production checkout on the first afternoon, because a missing export would then hide real work. The fixture should fit in a few files so the hash list stays readable in a later review. Can you name the single file this agent is allowed to touch before the run begins? 2. Write the refusal list first I write the tools I will not grant before I write the tools I might grant, because permission drift is how a sketch becomes a release. Network calls, package installs, and secret files stay off unless the task cannot be judged without them. If the free server cannot express that refusal in a file I keep, I do not use it beyond a demo. Would a screenshot of a settings toggle still survive your next incident review without the original account? 3. Run once, then pack before the diff I run the agent once, then I pack the bundle before I read the diff, so curiosity does not delay the export. The pack step hashes the workspace, copies the prompt, and checks that the tool log matches a small schema. If the pack step fails, the host has already told me it is a weak long-term seat. Why would I wait for a prettier second run to learn that the log never left the console? 4. Restore on a machine that did not work I restore the bundle on a second machine that did not perform the run, because a backup you never open is only a story. I check that the hashes match and that a human can see which command was refused. If restore works only while the original server is still up, I do not have custody of the run. Does your export button contain the log, or does it contain only the final patch? 5. Score the seat with four hard checks I score the seat on four yes-or-no checks, and a single no keeps that seat off any path that can merge. The checks are export without the host, restore without the host, refusal list in the bundle, and no secret in the log. A free server that passes all four checks can hold disposable drafts while I keep watching it. A free server that fails any one of them stays a whiteboard, even if the editor feels fast. Keep the fixture boring enough to hash I keep the fixture boring on purpose, so a failed hash points at custody rather than at a clever repository layout. The allowed edit lives under src, the failing test lives under tests, and the secrets directory is never mounted. If your agent host cannot exclude a path, write that down as a no before you admire any generated patch. Would you notice a secret read if the only record was a green checkmark in someone else's interface? fixture-repo/ README.md src/parse.py tests/test_parse.py secrets/ # forbidden path, never mounted refusal-list.txt # network, package_install, read_secret prompt.md tool-log.jsonl The following script is a proposal I have not executed against a live vendor for this draft, so treat every path as a local sketch. It assumes you already saved the prompt file, the refusal list, and the tool log beside the fixture repo. If your host will not let you save those files, stop and record that as a failed check. Would you rather discover the missing log in a script, or in a review three days later? # !/usr/bin/env bash # Proposal only. Not run against a live host for this draft. set -euo pipefail bundle_dir="${1:-./exit-bundle}" workspace="${2:-./fixture-repo}" mkdir -p "${bundle_dir}/workspace" cp -a "${workspace}/." "${bundle_dir}/workspace/" cp -a ./prompt.md "${bundle_dir}/prompt.md" cp -a ./refusal-list.txt "${bundle_dir}/refusal-list.txt" cp -a ./tool-log.jsonl "${bundle_dir}/tool-log.jsonl" find "${bundle_dir}/workspace" -type f -print0 | sort -z | xargs -0 sha256sum > "${bundle_dir}/workspace.sha256" python3 check_bundle.py "${bundle_dir}" # Proposal: local schema check. Not a vendor client and not a benchmark. import json import sys from pathlib import Path REQUIRED = ("ts", "tool", "status", "args_hash") def main(bundle: Path) -> int: log_path = bundle / "tool-log.jsonl" refused = (bundle / "refusal-list.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").split() lines = log_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() for line_no, line in enumerate(lines, 1): row = json.loads(line) missing = [key for key in REQUIRED if key not in row] if missing: print(f"line {line_no} missing {missing}") return 1 if row["tool"] in refused and row["status"] != "refused": print(f"line {line_no} ran a refused tool") return 1 print("bundle log passed the local checks") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main(Path(sys.argv[1]))) A sample log line I would accept looks like the JSON below, and I would reject a line that omits the status. I hash arguments instead of copying raw values, because a tool log should not become a second copy of your secrets. If the host only offers a pretty timeline in the browser, I transcribe nothing by hand and I fail the seat. Is a manual paste really an export, or is it a memory test with extra steps? {"ts":"2026-09-25T12:00:00Z","tool":"apply_patch","status":"ok","args_hash":"sha256:example"} On the second machine I only run two commands, because a restore ritual with twenty steps will not happen on a Friday. The hash check tells me the files arrived, and the Python check tells me the log still honors the refusal list. If either command fails, I stop the trial and I do not grant that seat a second, larger repository. How many hosts would you drop this week if a two-command restore was a required screenshot in review? sha256sum -c exit-bundle/workspace.sha256 python3 check_bundle.py exit-bundle Read the fit table as a gate I put the same four checks in a table so a reviewer can mark a seat without turning the drill into a debate. The rows are gates, and I do not let a friendly price column appear until the custody rows are filled. Self-hosted is not an automatic pass, because a disk you never restore is just a warmer sketchpad. Paid isolation is not an automatic pass either, unless the export survives after you cancel the session. CheckFree shared seatSelf-hosted seatPaid isolated seatExport without the host processOften unknown until you tryYes, if you own the diskOnly if the contract includes an exportRestore on a second machinePasses only after a real drillPasses if backups are realPasses if the image is portableRefusal list stored in the bundleWeak if toggles are UI-onlyStrong if you keep the fileStrong if policy is exportableSecret leakage in logsYour job to prove a noYour job to prove a noYour job to prove a noGood fitDisposable drafts and spikesTeams who already operate the boxTeams who need a vendor boundaryPoor fitRelease branches and secretsTeams with no backup habitBuyers who never test restore I read that table as a gate, not as a score I can average into a comforting total. One failed custody check is enough to keep that seat away from any merge queue I run. Price can break a tie after the checks pass, but it cannot repair a missing log. If two seats both pass, I then ask which one my teammate can operate during my week off. Where a free hosted project fits I apply the same gate to hosted projects, including MonkeyCode, instead of granting a pass because the seat is described as free. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator describes MonkeyCode as an open-source project that currently offers free model access and a free server option. I am not quoting a token allowance, hardware shape, model list, or end date in this draft. This draft was not given a primary page I could cite, so I refuse to invent a quota or a duration. Read the project documentation on the day you decide, and keep only the figures that page still shows. A free model lane can be a fair place to rehearse the fixture while the refusal list still changes hourly. A free server seat can be a fair place to learn whether export is even possible before you trust the seat. Neither offer, as described to me, replaces the restore drill or a disk you control for release work. If the current docs confirm a free lane, I would still pack the bundle before that lane sees anything beyond the fixture. A passing fixture on Monday does not promote the seat, because Monday fixtures are supposed to stay disposable. If you review runs by leftover files, try this drill on the free seat you are curious about. Limits, and who should walk away This drill does not measure model quality, latency, or cost per accepted patch, so a green restore is not wisdom. I have not timed the script, I have not compared vendors, and I will not invent numbers to finish the table. The schema is intentionally small, and a real team may need identity, revision, and approval fields. If your auditor needs those fields, extend the check before you trust a passing printout from the script. You should not use a shared free seat for regulated data, customer repositories, or a workspace that must stay on a named network. You should not use this approach if you cannot spare a second machine, because an unopened bundle is not custody. You should also skip it when your real question is which model writes better prose, since this gate never answers that. I would rather fail a convenient seat on Tuesday than explain a vanished log to the team on Friday. What I want from the next host I try is a folder I can hash and a refusal list I can diff. I also want a restore that does not beg the original server to stay online after I close the tab. If a free option gives me that folder, I will use it for drafts without pretending it is a permanent home. If it does not, I will pay for or assemble the seat that does, and I will keep the fixture as the receipt. So which seat are you actually able to leave tonight, with the log in your hand rather than in a tab? If the answer is none of them, the honest next hour is the fixture, not another signup. I would rather spend that hour packing a boring bundle than arguing about a host I cannot exit. Does that sound slow, or does it sound like the first review you would want after a bad patch lands? # ai # devops # tutorial # testing # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community Decide the Agent Seat by the Bundle You Can Carry Out
